claims.claim: 100 lookups a second is a light load. One Python process doing sub-millisecond work can handle several times that.
claims.measured: On 1 CPU: python-flask 1,732 req/s plaintext and 1,700 JSON; python-flask-gthread about 4,000; python-fastapi 7,442 plaintext and 6,732 JSON; with fib(20) CPU work per request, Python servers managed about 1,050–1,260 req/s
claims.why: The claim is a floor of a few hundred requests a second per process, and every measured Python setup clears it, at about 1,000–7,400 req/s on one CPU even with CPU work per request.

claims.claim: Finding one variant or a region is a binary search, which takes microseconds in NumPy
claims.why: The benchmark measures web request handling and doesn't time NumPy searchsorted or any in-memory index lookup.

claims.claim: The 50 ms budget will mostly go on network time and turning results into JSON, not on the search
claims.why: The measurements only give latency for tiny JSON payloads under saturating load, so they can't show how a request's time splits between network, serialization and search at 100 req/s.

claims.claim: Rewriting the service in C++, Rust or Go would be fast, but no faster in any way users would notice
claims.measured: At saturation, rust-actix does 86,102 req/s plaintext (p50 0.72 ms) against 1,732 for python-flask (p50 35.55 ms) and 7,442 for python-fastapi (p50 7.46 ms)
claims.why: The large measured gaps are at saturating load, and the benchmark doesn't measure latency at a light load of about 100 req/s, which is where the claim about what users would notice applies.

claims.claim: With several gunicorn workers, each one loads its own 4 GB, so 4 workers would fill all 16 GB
claims.why: Measured peak memory covers only trivial handlers of about 55–123 MB for Flask, not a process holding a 4 GB in-memory dataset.

claims.claim: Turning 100,000 variants into JSON will take far longer than 50 ms
claims.why: The JSON test serializes one small object per request, so it says nothing about the cost of serializing 100,000 records.
